findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is visible to anyone with instance metadata access or console/API describe permissions, leading to credential leakage.
The instance is deployed into a subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch enabled and attached to a security group allowing inbound SSH and HTTP from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing it directly to the internet.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, so data stored on it is unencrypted at rest, risking exposure if the underlying storage is compromised or snapshots are shared.
The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted volume and has no encryption specified, meaning the snapshot data (and any copies or shares of it) remains unencrypted at rest.
Ingress rule allows TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, permitting SSH access attempts from any host on the internet.
Ingress rule allows TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no additional protections (e.g., no TLS/HTTPS enforcement), exposing the web service broadly and enabling cleartext HTTP traffic.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing all instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing all instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet.
The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.
The S3 bucket has no public access block or bucket policy defined, and force_destroy is enabled, leaving it potentially open to misconfiguration-driven public exposure of flow log data.
